1.e4 c6 2.d4.strategy: Builds a two-pawn centre and takes the most space. Black's 2...d5 attacks e4 at once, and White then decides the character of the game: open piece play, a closed centre where White holds the space, or a balanced structure after an exchange. The cost is a centre that Black challenges straight away.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and keeps the d-pawn flexible, so White can still head for the main line or choose faster development with the knights. The price is that the knight occupies c3, which rules out a set-up with the c-pawn on c3.

1.e4 c6 2.c4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Accelerated Panov Attack
1.e4 c6 2.c4.background: After 2...d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.d4 it transposes to the Panov–Botvinnik Attack, named after Vasily Panov and world champion Mikhail Botvinnik, which otherwise begins 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4. The position after 2.c4 can also arise from the English Opening, after 1.c4 c6 2.e4.
1.e4 c6 2.c4.strategy: Controls d5 in advance, so that White can meet 2...d5 by exchanging and then striking at the centre with d4, aiming for open, active play. The move develops no piece, and Black can sidestep these structures by building the centre differently.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight toward the centre and keeps the d-pawn flexible, aiming at quick development. It leaves e4 undefended for the moment, so White has to deal with the attack on it after 2...d5, but the queen's knight stays free to choose its square.

1.e4 c6 2.d3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Breyer Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d3.background: White more often answers 2...d5 with 3.Nd2, but the queenless line 3.Nf3 dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1 gained attention in the 21st century.
1.e4 c6 2.d3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn and prepares quiet development of the pieces. It is sound but unambitious: White postpones the fight for d4 and aims for a slow, flexible game in which the queens often stay on the board.

1.e4 c6 2.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 with pawn support. The move is sound but rare: it takes c3 from the queen's knight, which can no longer defend e4 from there.

1.e4 c6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2 and keeps d4 and Nc3 in reserve. It is sound but slow: after 2...d5 the e4-pawn needs an answer at once, and the bishop on g2 bears on the centre only after that pawn has been exchanged or advanced.

1.e4 c6 2.b3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Euwe Attack
1.e4 c6 2.b3.background: Max Euwe won with it against Richard Réti in the third game of their match in Amsterdam in June 1920.
1.e4 c6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2 on the long diagonal and fights for the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. It leaves Black free to build a broad centre, and White has to undermine that centre later.

1.e4 c6 2.f3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn but takes f3 from the king's knight and weakens the e1–h4 and a7–g1 diagonals. Black can also answer 2...e5, aiming at the dark squares around White's king.

1.e4 c6 2.e5.strategy: Pushes the e-pawn before d4 can support it, so 2...d6 hits the pawn at once. White has gained space only if Black allows it.

1.e4 c6 2.Ne2.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Bohemian Attack
1.e4 c6 2.Ne2.strategy: Blocks the f1-bishop and does not defend e4, so 2...d5 attacks the pawn at once. The knight covers d4 and can reroute to g3, but White develops more slowly than after the natural knight moves.

1.e4 c6 2.Be2.strategy: A slow developing move that neither supports e4 nor prepares d4, and takes e2 from the queen and the g1-knight. Black takes the centre with 2...d5, and the bishop on e2 does nothing against it.

1.e4 c6 2.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 but blocks the d2-pawn, so d4 is impossible until the bishop moves again. Black takes the centre with 2...d5, and after ...dxe4 Bxe4 the bishop is hit by ...Nf6 with gain of time.

1.e4 c6 2.Bc4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Hillbilly Attack
1.e4 c6 2.Bc4.background: Simon Williams attributes the name to National Master Jack Young, who allegedly used it for the move's unrefined nature and claimed to have invented it in 1988. It emerged as a surprise weapon in online blitz because of the gambit 3.Bb3 after 2...d5, advocated by Williams.
1.e4 c6 2.Bc4.strategy: Aims at f7 but the bishop is hit by 2...d5, and after 3.exd5 cxd5 it has to move again, losing time. White gets no lasting initiative for the tempo and Black takes the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.g4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Spike Variation
1.e4 c6 2.g4.strategy: Advances on the kingside without developing a piece and weakens the squares around the king. Black strikes at e4 with 2...d5, and the g4-pawn becomes a target for the c8-bishop and for ...h5.

1.e4 c6 2.b4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Labahn Attack
1.e4 c6 2.b4.strategy: Gains queenside space without developing and leaves the b4-pawn unsupported. Black takes the centre at once and can harass the unprotected pawn.

1.e4 c6 2.f4.strategy: Gains kingside space and prepares Nf3 and e5, but weakens the e1–h4 diagonal and the e3-square. It does nothing for e4, so 2...d5 attacks an undefended pawn and Black develops easily.

1.e4 c6 2.Qf3.strategy: Defends e4 but takes f3 from the king's knight and exposes the queen early. After 2...d5 the c8-bishop can hit the queen from g4, so Black develops with gain of time.

1.e4 c6 2.Qe2.strategy: Defends e4 but shuts in the f1-bishop and takes e2 from the king's knight, while d4 remains unprepared. Black takes the centre with 2...d5 and develops freely.

1.e4 c6 2.Qg4.strategy: Loses time: after 2...d5 the c8-bishop attacks the queen, which must retreat, and 3.exd5? even loses it to 3...Bxg4. Black gets the centre and development with tempo.

1.e4 c6 2.Qh5.strategy: Eyes f7, but the queen is exposed: 2...Nf6 attacks it and the e4-pawn at the same time, and Black develops with gain of time.

1.e4 c6 2.Nh3.strategy: Develops the king's knight to the rim, where it neither defends e4 nor supports d4. After 2...d5 the c8-bishop also hits the knight, and ...Bxh3 gxh3 would double White's h-pawns.

1.e4 c6 2.Na3.strategy: A rim knight that helps neither e4 nor d4. It heads for c4, but 2...d5 takes that square away at once, and White has lost time without a plan.

1.e4 c6 2.a3.strategy: A slow rook-pawn move that neither develops a piece nor fights for the centre. Black takes space at once with 2...d5 and has gained a tempo.

1.e4 c6 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space slowly and weakens b4, but does nothing against 2...d5, which takes the centre with a tempo against e4.

1.e4 c6 2.h3.strategy: A waiting move that only prevents ...Bg4 later. It costs a tempo and does nothing about 2...d5, so Black takes the centre while White has not developed.

1.e4 c6 2.h4.strategy: Gains a little kingside space but neither develops a piece nor helps the centre. Black takes the centre with 2...d5, attacking the undefended e4-pawn, and White is a tempo behind.

1.e4 c6 2.Ke2.strategy: Gives up castling for good and leaves the king in the centre, with no gain in space or development. Black plays 2...d5 and opens the centre against the exposed king.

1.e4 c6 2.Bb5.strategy: Hangs the bishop: the c6-pawn simply takes it with 2...cxb5.

1.e4 c6 2.Ba6.strategy: Hangs the bishop for nothing: 2...bxa6 or 2...Nxa6 wins it at once.

1.e4 c6.name: Caro–Kann Defence
1.e4 c6.background: Named after the English player Horatio Caro and the Austrian Marcus Kann, who analysed it in 1886. Kann had beaten Jacques Mieses with it in 24 moves at the German Chess Congress in Hamburg in May 1885.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 at once, which is the point of the c6 pawn: it supports d5, so Black recaptures with a pawn and keeps a sound structure. Unlike in the French, the c8-bishop is not shut in. The cost is the tempo spent on ...c6, so Black can lag in development; the game is usually solid and positional.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 Na6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: De Bruycker Defence
1.e4 c6 2.d4 Na6.strategy: Heads for c7 via a6, where the knight supports d5 and e6 without blocking the c8-bishop. The price is an extra tempo and a knight that stands on the rim for a move, so White builds the centre at leisure and stays slightly ahead in development.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 Nf6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Masi Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 and invites White to push e5, driving the knight back; a following c4 chases it again and gives White a broad centre, while ...c6 adds little. If White simply defends e4 instead, ...d5 is met by e5, again gaining time on the knight.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d6.strategy: Heads for a compact, flexible set-up with ...c6 already included. It concedes more central space than ...d5 does and leaves White free to build a broad centre or to develop calmly. Sound but passive.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and keeps the choice open between a Caro–Kann structure and a more compact set-up. Sound and flexible, but less direct than ...d5, and it leaves White free to build a broad centre.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid pawn chain, ...c6 already inserted, which supports d5 but shuts the c8-bishop in behind e6. Black also loses the quick ...c5 break that normally frees such a chain, so the c6 pawn costs a tempo.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 Qc7.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece; on c7 it eyes e5 but does nothing for ...d5. White develops freely, and once the c-pawn leaves c6, Nb5 can hit the queen.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 Qb6.strategy: Hits d4 and b2 only on paper, since Qd1 and Bc1 cover them. White gains tempi against the queen, while ...d5 has still not been played.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 Qa5+.strategy: The check achieves nothing: White blocks it with a developing or centre-strengthening move, and the queen is left loose on a5 with ...d5 still unplayed.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it invites 3.Bxh6 gxh6 and a ruined kingside pawn structure, and does nothing about the centre. Black keeps the bishop pair after the trade, but White's centre goes unchallenged.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 a6.strategy: A waiting move on the edge that prepares ...b5 but contests nothing. White develops freely or takes more space, while ...d5 is still to be played.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook's pawn while d4 and e4 stand unopposed, and the a-pawn can no longer cover b5 from a6, a hole once the c-pawn leaves c6. White simply builds up.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but there the bishop bites on its own pawn on c6, and ...d5 is still unplayed. White develops freely, and freeing the bishop with ...c5 costs Black another tempo.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 b5.strategy: Grabs queenside space before the centre is settled, weakening c6 and c5 and leaving the b-pawn as a target for a4. Nothing is done against d4 and e4, and White develops freely.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 e5.strategy: Strikes at d4 before the pieces are out. After 3.dxe5 Black regains the pawn most directly with ...Qa5+ and ...Qxe5, but the queen is then exposed to Nf3 and Bf4 while White develops with tempo.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the g8-knight, weakens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal, and does not fight for the centre. White simply builds up.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 f5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Massachusetts Defence
1.e4 c6 2.d4 f5.strategy: Weakens e6, the e8–h5 diagonal and the kingside without developing anything. After 3.exf5 Black regains the pawn most directly with ...Qa5+ and ...Qxf5, and Nc3 followed by Bd3 gains a tempo on the queen; 3.e5 simply takes space.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 h6.strategy: Stops Bg5 but is a pure waiting move on the rim. It loses time and does not contest d4 or e4, so White builds freely while ...d5 waits.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 h5.strategy: Pushes the rook's pawn without contesting d4 or e4 and loosens g5 and g6. White develops freely while Black has still to deal with the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 c5.strategy: Moves the same pawn a second time and lets White take space or open the centre. If White takes on c5, ...Qa5+ and ...Qxc5 regain the pawn, but with the queen out early and White ahead in development.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn to 3.Bxg5, since neither the queen nor the f8-bishop covers it, and loosens the kingside for nothing.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 at once, and the c6 pawn already guards d5, so Black can recapture there without loosening anything. Black keeps a solid structure with the light-squared bishop free, at the cost of a slower start in development, since the c-pawn has already moved.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks e4, but the knight becomes a target for the e-pawn. After 3.d4 the natural 3...d5 runs into 4.e5, gaining time, and 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nxd5 cxd5 5.d4 at once gives White a space advantage with the pawn on e5.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Prepares ...Nf6 and a compact, flexible set-up that keeps the centre open to several plans. It is sound but passive: White takes the full centre before Black contests it.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with ...c6 already played, a set-up that supports d5 but shuts the c8 bishop in behind e6. After 3.d4 d5 4.e5 Black wants the ...c5 break against White's pawn chain, and the pawn on c6 needs a second move to get there. Solid, but 2...d5 at once keeps the bishop free.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 with ...c6 already played and leaves Black the choice between a solid pawn centre and a more elastic set-up. Sound and flexible, but it gives White more options than the direct 2...d5.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Strikes in the centre, but ...c6 has taken the b8 knight's natural square and e5 lacks support. After 3.Nf3 Black usually has to spend another tempo defending e5, because 3...d5 4.exd5 cxd5 5.Nxe5 loses a pawn.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Qc7.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece; on c7 it supports ...e5 but does nothing for ...d5. White takes the centre at once and builds on it, while Black still has all four minor pieces to develop.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Qb6.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece and eyes b2, which the c1 bishop guards. White gains time against the queen by attacking it with the a-pawn or the knight.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Qa5.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece and eyes the c3 knight, which the b- and d-pawns guard. After 3.d4 the knight is pinned, but Bd2 can break the pin at any time, and White builds the centre further while the queen has nothing to attack.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, from where it can reach f5 to press on d4 but does nothing against e4. Once White plays d4, the c1 bishop can take with Bxh6 gxh6, doubling Black's h-pawns, although Black gets the bishop pair in return.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, from where it heads for c7 to support ...d5. 3.Bxa6 bxa6 doubles Black's a-pawns at once, at the cost of the bishop pair, and White can also take the centre while the knight is still on its way.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that prepares ...b5 but develops nothing and does not contest e4. White takes the centre at once and develops freely, while ...d5 has still to be played.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook's pawn and does nothing against e4 or for ...d5. White takes the centre at once and develops freely.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but the c6 pawn blocks that bishop's diagonal, so the fianchetto has little to aim at. It costs a tempo while White takes the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Grabs queenside space but develops nothing, and the pawn, already hit by the c3 knight, ties the c6 pawn to its defence. After 3.d4 d5 4.exd5, for instance, 4...cxd5 drops the b-pawn to 5.Bxb5+ or 5.Nxb5.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Covers e5 but takes the natural f6 square from the g8 knight and opens the e8–h5 diagonal, so Qh5+ is possible at any moment. White develops freely and aims at the weakened a2–g8 diagonal.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside without developing anything. After 3.d4 the c1 bishop attacks g5, so Black must spend another move holding the pawn, and after 3...h6 it comes under fire again from 4.h4.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a pawn move that stops a bishop which cannot yet come to g5, and does nothing for the centre. 3.d4 gives White the centre with a free hand.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Pushes the rook's pawn without contesting e4 and loosens g5 and g6. White takes the centre at once and develops freely.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Moves the c-pawn a second time and reaches the position after 1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 with White to move, so Black has lost a whole tempo. White can develop and open the centre with d4 a move ahead.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: Gives up a pawn: after 3.exf5 nothing recaptures on f5, and 3...d5? runs into 4.Qh5+ g6 5.fxg6. After 3...Nf6 White can hold the extra pawn with 4.g4.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d5.strategy: Strikes at the e4-pawn at once, the thematic Caro–Kann break, before White can support the centre. White then chooses how the pawns are exchanged, and in the main lines ends up with an isolated d-pawn, accepted for fast development and attacking chances.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 d6.strategy: Postpones the ...d5 break for a compact set-up with pawns on c6 and d6. It is solid but passive: with pawns on c4, d4 and e4 White gets a clear space advantage, and Black has to catch up from behind.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a French-style pawn chain. It is sound, but it shuts in the c8-bishop that the Caro–Kann set-up usually keeps free, and White's extra space on c4 gives the more comfortable play.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 e5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Accelerated Panov Attack, Open Variation
1.e4 c6 2.c4 e5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn instead of striking at e4 with ...d5. The c6-pawn takes the natural square from the knight, so Black must keep e5 defended, and with c4 and e4 covering d5 the freeing ...d5 is hard to achieve. The position stays solid but passive.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, with ...c6 already played. It is sound but leaves the centre to White: with pawns on c4, d4 and e4 White has a clear space advantage, and Black must find the right moment for ...d5.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, far from the centre, aiming at c7 or b4. It does nothing against a broad pawn centre, so White simply builds one while c4 and e4 keep their grip on d5.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Qc7.strategy: Eyes e5 along the b8–h2 diagonal but brings the queen out before any piece is developed. White takes the centre at leisure, and Bf4 can later gain time against the queen.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Qb6.strategy: Aims at b2 and d4, but b2 is guarded by the c1-bishop, so nothing is threatened. The queen leaves the back rank before any piece is developed, and White builds a full centre in comfort.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Qa5.strategy: Eyes the a5–e1 diagonal and prepares ...e5, but develops nothing. White gains time developing, and the queen stays exposed to harassment by ideas such as Bd2.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Nh6.strategy: A rim knight aiming at f5 that leaves d5 uncontested. Once White plays d4, Bxh6 gxh6 threatens to wreck the kingside pawns, so Black must spend more time on the knight or the kingside.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 but runs into 3.e5, which drives the knight away. White gains space and tempi, and Black's pieces stand awkwardly in the face of a broad centre.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 against the c4-pawn but spends a tempo on an edge pawn. White builds a broad centre while ...d5 is still unplayed.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 a5.strategy: A wing move that gains no useful space and touches neither the centre nor the d5 square. White builds on the pawns already on c4 and e4.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but the c6-pawn blocks that bishop's diagonal toward e4, and ...d5 still has to be played. White meanwhile takes the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 f6.strategy: Blocks the knight's natural square and weakens e6 and the king's diagonal. It does nothing against the pawns on c4 and e4, and White takes the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside for good and makes the pawn a target: after d4 the c1-bishop attacks g5, and holding it with ...h6 costs another tempo against White's full centre.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 h6.strategy: A prophylactic pawn move that takes g5 from the bishop but develops nothing and leaves d5 uncontested. White builds a broad centre.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 h5.strategy: Gains space on the wing but weakens g5 and the kingside, and develops nothing. White keeps the centre and develops freely.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 c5.strategy: The second step of the c-pawn gives a Sicilian-like structure but costs a tempo, and with c4 and e4 White already controls d5. A quiet bind follows easily.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn without real compensation. After 3.cxb5 cxb5 4.Bxb5 White is a clean pawn up, and the open c-file and ...Bb7 against e4 do not make up for it.

1.e4 c6 2.c4 f5.strategy: Offers the f-pawn for nothing: 3.exf5 simply wins it, and the king and the e6-square are left weakened with no development in return.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 at once, the point of the Caro-Kann: the c6 pawn backs d5, so if White takes, Black recaptures with the c-pawn and keeps a healthy centre pawn and a half-open c-file. If White pushes e5 instead, Black can bring out the light-squared bishop before closing its diagonal. The price is a tempo spent on ...c6, in return for a solid structure.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: Backs up a later ...d5, but closes the c8-bishop's diagonal before the bishop is out. If White gets a pawn to e5, the bishop stays shut in behind a French-like pawn chain. Sound, but it gives up the Caro-Kann's chief idea of developing that bishop first.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 and invites White to push e5 and chase the knight. Black gets a sound game, but White gains space while the knight is driven about, so it is less comfortable than the direct ...d5.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Prepares a set-up with pawns on c6 and d6 against a broad White centre, instead of challenging it with ...d5. Solid and flexible, but passive: Black cedes space and the initiative.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and to undermine White's centre later, instead of fighting for it now. Sound, but less direct than ...d5, and White takes the centre unopposed.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Reaches the Sicilian pawn structure at the cost of a tempo: the same position with Black to move would be an ordinary Sicilian, so White has an Open Sicilian with Black a move behind.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim on its way to c7, where it would support ...d5, but spends a tempo while ...d5 is still undone. White gets a lead in development and central space.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 Qc7.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece; on c7 it eyes e5 but does nothing for ...d5. White develops with gain of time and takes space.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 Qb6.strategy: Attacks b2 and f2, but the c1-bishop and the king guard them, so there is no threat. The queen becomes a target for attack, and White develops with tempo while ...d5 is still undone.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 Qa5.strategy: Pins the d2 pawn against the king, so White cannot play d4 for a move, but blocking the diagonal with a piece or pawn ends the pin. The queen stands exposed on a5, and Black has still not moved a central pawn.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 from the rim, but White's d4 opens the c1-h6 diagonal, and Bxh6 forces ...gxh6 and wrecks the kingside pawns. The knight also stays off f6, and ...d5 is still undone.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn: with c6 already covering b5, the move only prepares ...b5, which does nothing for the centre. White takes space and develops.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space for a tempo but does nothing for the centre or development, and leaves b6 without a pawn guard.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares a queenside fianchetto, but a bishop on b7 would face its own c6 pawn and be blocked, and the centre is left to White.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Throws the b-pawn forward before the centre is settled: a4 hits it at once, and the pawns on b5 and c6 loosen the queenside without helping development.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the knight, opens the e8-h5 diagonal and weakens e6, while doing nothing for ...d5. White builds a centre at leisure, and Black lags in development.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's knight and bishop but spends a tempo on a pawn move that does nothing for the centre. White builds a centre with a free hand.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Gains kingside space, but the h-pawn can no longer cover g5 from h6, and the move does nothing for development or the centre. White simply builds a centre.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 e5.strategy: Offers a pawn that nothing defends: Nxe5 takes it, and Black regains it with ...Qe7 and ...Qxe4+ only by bringing the queen out early, which hands White a lead in development.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal for a pawn that exf5 takes at once. Black can win it back, but is left with a hole on e6 and a backward e7 pawn on the half-open e-file.

1.e4 c6 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Hangs the pawn to Nxg5, which nothing defends, and weakens f5, h5 and the whole kingside for good.
